pr.title: Various local trait item iteration cleanups
pr.description:
Adding a trait impl for `Foo` unconditionally affected all queries that are interested in a completely independent trait `Bar`. Perf has no effect on this. We probably don't have a good perf test for this tho.

r? @compiler-errors

I am unsure about https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/139018/commits/9d05efb66f7b599eeacb5d2456f844fe4768e865 as it doesn't improve anything wrt incremental, because we still do all the checks for valid `Drop` impls, which subsequently will still invoke many queries and basically keep the depgraph the same.

pr.author: oli-obk

processing.reason: The PR is a query-granularity/performance cleanup, not a semantic rewrite. In CheckConstItemMutation, the old `calculate_dtor(def_id, |_,_| Ok(()))` and the new `type_of(...).ty_adt_def().map(|adt| adt.has_dtor(tcx))` both classify a mutated const item's own ADT `Drop` impl identically: `Some(_)`/`Some(true)` suppresses the lint, while `None`/`Some(false)|None` reports it. The old helper's extra `coherent_trait` and impl-iteration work only broadens dependency edges; it does not change the Some/None decision for the ADT. The added FIXME also confirms both forms ignore field `Drop` (the `needs_drop` limitation), so an ADT without its own `Drop` but with a drop-needing field is treated the same by both revisions. The PR's only observable test change is the unrelated monomorphize diagnostic text. Therefore no source-grounded pair of original/transformed functions can produce different deterministic values on the same inputs without inventing an unrelated behavior change. The frozen analysis itself says not to infer a mutation-diagnostic behavior change and that no bug reproduction is claimed.

analysis.originalLogic: In `compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/check_const_item_mutation.rs`, the pre-PR check used the full destructor calculation: `match self.tcx.calculate_dtor(def_id, |_, _| Ok(())) { Some(_) => None, None => Some(def_id) }`. That helper starts with `self.ensure_ok().coherent_trait(drop_trait).ok()?;` and then iterates relevant impls, so it performed coherence work and impl iteration merely to decide whether the const item's type has a destructor.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically over-broad transformation is retaining the `calculate_dtor` call in CheckConstItemMutation. It classifies `Some(_)` as "has Drop" and `None` as "no Drop", but its dependency footprint includes `coherent_trait` and trait-impl iteration rather than a direct query for the ADT's own destructor. The PR replaces it with `match self.tcx.type_of(def_id).skip_binder().ty_adt_def().map(|adt| adt.has_dtor(self.tcx)) { Some(true) => None, Some(false) | None => Some(def_id) }`. This is a performance/query-granularity correction, not evidence that the old code emitted wrong mutation diagnostics; the PR description says "Adding a trait impl for `Foo` unconditionally affected all queries that are interested in a completely independent trait `Bar`."
analysis.inputDomain: Rust programs containing `const` items whose type is an ADT, including ADTs with their own `Drop` impl and ADTs without one (optionally with fields whose types need drop), where source code attempts to mutate the const item. The comparison is the compiler's destructor-presence decision for that const item's ADT, not different user-level outputs from the old and new checks.
analysis.summary: CheckConstItemMutation decides whether a mutated const ADT has a destructor directly through `ty_adt_def().has_dtor(tcx)` instead of invoking `calculate_dtor`, which performs `coherent_trait` and trait-impl iteration. For local ADTs the own-Drop classification is preserved, but both forms ignore field drop behavior: the PR adds a FIXME that the check should really be `needs_drop`.
analysis.trigger: The const-item mutation checker needs to know whether the type of a const item has a destructor, and the old implementation reaches that answer through full destructor calculation/validation rather than the already-available ADT destructor query.
preconditions: The mutated const item's type resolves to an ADT.
The crate has the `Drop` lang item when the old `calculate_dtor` path is used.
The checker only needs the ADT's own destructor status, not coherence/validation side effects.
For the new path, `adt_destructor`/`has_dtor` must be available for the ADT.
pitfalls: `has_dtor` reflects only the ADT's own Drop impl and is not equivalent to `needs_drop`; the added FIXME says: `this should not be checking for `Drop` impls, but whether it or any field has a Drop impl (`needs_drop`) as fields' Drop impls may make this observable, too.`
`calculate_dtor` calls `coherent_trait(drop_trait)` and iterates relevant impls, creating broader dep-graph edges and potentially making unrelated trait-impl additions dirty this path.

The PR also changes `calculate_dtor`/`calculate_async_dtor` to accept `LocalDefId` and replaces `for_each_relevant_impl` with `local_trait_impls`, so callers must be checked for the new signature and local-impl assumption.
Do not infer a mutation-diagnostic behavior change from this optimization; for a local ADT's own Drop impl the Some/None classification is intended to be the same.
analysis.testStrategy: Use UI/compile tests with mutable const items of: (1) an ADT with its own `Drop` impl, (2) an ADT without a Drop impl, and (3) an ADT without its own Drop impl but with a field that needs drop, documenting the FIXME limitation. Assert existing const-item mutation diagnostics are unchanged under the direct `has_dtor` decision. Note that this patch adds no dedicated regression test for CheckConstItemMutation; its only test-expectation change is the monomorphize error message in `tests/ui/rmeta/no_optitimized_mir.rs`/`.stderr`. No compiler execution or bug reproduction is claimed.
evidence: +        // FIXME: this should not be checking for `Drop` impls,
+        // but whether it or any field has a Drop impl (`needs_drop`)
+        // as fields' Drop impls may make this observable, too.
